title: One lot for the Lord, the other “for the scapegoat”: for what, or for whom, is the second lot?
summary: Two lots are cast over two goats. One is “for the Lord”. The KJV says the other is “for the scapegoat”. The Hebrew has a word, azazel, that stands where “the Lord” stands in the first half of the sentence. The KJV has “scapegoat” in this chapter only. The passage does not say what the word means.
text: KJV Leviticus 16:8: “And Aaron shall cast lots upon the two goats; one lot for the Lord, and the other lot for the scapegoat.” KJV 16:10: “But the goat, on which the lot fell to be the scapegoat, shall be presented alive before the Lord, to make an atonement with him, and to let him go for a scapegoat into the wilderness.” KJV 16:21: “and shall send him away by the hand of a fit man into the wilderness” KJV 16:22: “And the goat shall bear upon him all their iniquities unto a land not inhabited: and he shall let go the goat in the wilderness.” KJV 16:26: “And he that let go the goat for the scapegoat shall wash his clothes” Hebrew (WLC) 16:8: גֹּורָ֤ל אֶחָד֙ לַיהוָ֔ה וְגֹורָ֥ל אֶחָ֖ד לַעֲזָאזֵֽל [one lot for the LORD and one lot for azazel]. 16:10: לְשַׁלַּ֥ח אֹתֹ֛ו לַעֲזָאזֵ֖ל הַמִּדְבָּֽרָה [to send it away to azazel, to the wilderness]. 16:26: וְהַֽמְשַׁלֵּ֤חַ אֶת־הַשָּׂעִיר֙ לַֽעֲזָאזֵ֔ל [and he who sends away the goat to azazel]. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) 16:8: κλῆρον ἕνα τῷ Κυρίῳ, καὶ κλῆρον ἕνα τῷ ἀποπομπαίῳ [one lot for the Lord and one lot for the one of the sending away]. 16:10: ὥστε ἀποστεῖλαι αὐτὸν εἰς τὴν ἀποπομπήν [so as to send it out for the sending away]. 16:26: τὸν χίμαρον τὸν διεσταλμένον εἰς ἄφεσιν [the goat set apart for release]. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/3/16/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/LEV16.htm.
reasoning: The whole rite of the second goat turns on this word: the lot is cast for it, the goat is sent to it, and the man who leads the goat is described by it. Yet the chapter never explains it. In the KJV the lot falls “for the scapegoat”, though the goat is the thing the lot is cast upon. In the Hebrew the word is set in parallel with “for the LORD”. Whether the second lot is for a being, for a place, or for the act of removal changes what the rite is said to do.
scope: Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. Readings that have been proposed, none of which the chapter states: that the word describes the goat itself, as the goat that goes away, which is how the KJV takes it; that it names the place or the kind of place the goat is sent to, beside “a land not inhabited” in 16:22; that it means the removal itself, which is near the Greek of 16:10 and 16:26; or that it names a being set over against the LORD in 16:8. Check made: a search of the packaged KJV finds “scapegoat” in Leviticus 16:8, 16:10 and 16:26 only, and the Hebrew word was looked for in those three verses only; no search of the whole Hebrew Bible was run in this session. These checked verses do not explicitly settle which reading applies. A published record on the two goats’ roles already says that the meaning of the word needs further research; this record sets out the wording in the three texts. No H or G is proposed: no one meaning of the Hebrew is shown here, and the Greek of 16:8 is close to the KJV. The Hebrew quoted is the Westminster Leningrad Codex digital text. A digital named edition is not proof that every manuscript agrees; other Hebrew manuscripts were not examined. The Greek is Brenton’s printed edition of the Septuagint, an ancient Greek translation tradition of the Old Testament. It is not a critical apparatus and does not show that all Greek witnesses agree or which reading is original. title: “The morrow after the sabbath”: which sabbath starts the count of fifty days?
summary: The sheaf of firstfruits is waved “on the morrow after the sabbath”, and fifty days are counted from that day to the next feast. The passage gives every other feast a day of the month. It does not say which sabbath is meant, so the date of the sheaf, and of the feast fifty days later, is left open.
text: KJV Leviticus 23:6: “And on the fifteenth day of the same month is the feast of unleavened bread unto the Lord” KJV 23:7: “In the first day ye shall have an holy convocation: ye shall do no servile work therein.” KJV 23:8: “in the seventh day is an holy convocation” KJV 23:10: “When ye be come into the land which I give unto you, and shall reap the harvest thereof, then ye shall bring a sheaf of the firstfruits of your harvest unto the priest” KJV 23:11: “And he shall wave the sheaf before the Lord, to be accepted for you: on the morrow after the sabbath the priest shall wave it.” KJV 23:15: “And ye shall count unto you from the morrow after the sabbath, from the day that ye brought the sheaf of the wave offering; seven sabbaths shall be complete:” KJV 23:16: “Even unto the morrow after the seventh sabbath shall ye number fifty days; and ye shall offer a new meat offering unto the Lord.” KJV 23:39: “on the first day shall be a sabbath, and on the eighth day shall be a sabbath” KJV Joshua 5:11: “And they did eat of the old corn of the land on the morrow after the passover, unleavened cakes, and parched corn in the selfsame day.” Hebrew (WLC) 23:11: מִֽמָּחֳרַת֙ הַשַּׁבָּ֔ת [on the morrow of the sabbath]. 23:16: עַ֣ד מִֽמָּחֳרַ֤ת הַשַּׁבָּת֙ הַשְּׁבִיעִ֔ת [until the morrow of the seventh sabbath]. 23:39: בַּיֹּ֤ום הָֽרִאשֹׁון֙ שַׁבָּתֹ֔ון [on the first day a shabbathon, a related but different noun]. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) 23:11: τῇ ἐπαύριον τῆς πρώτης [on the morrow of the first]. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/3/23/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/LEV23.htm.
reasoning: Passover, unleavened bread, trumpets, atonement and tabernacles are each given a day of a month in this chapter. The sheaf and the feast fifty days after it are not: they hang on “the sabbath”. Nothing in 23:9–16 says whether this is the weekly sabbath that falls in the week of unleavened bread, the first day of that feast, its seventh day, or the first weekly sabbath after harvest begins. Each choice gives a different day for the sheaf, and so a different day for the feast that follows.
scope: Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. Readings, none of which the passage states: the weekly sabbath, so that the sheaf is always waved on the first day of the week; the first day of unleavened bread, a day of no servile work, so that the sheaf falls on a fixed day of the month, which is what Brenton’s Greek of 23:11 says and which is treated in a separate G record; or the seventh day of that feast. The KJV of 23:39 uses “a sabbath” for the first and eighth days of another feast, which shows the English word is not kept to the weekly day in this chapter; the Hebrew noun there is a different form from the one in 23:11. Joshua 5:11 tells of eating parched corn “on the morrow after the passover” and does not mention the sheaf or a sabbath, so it does not settle the question. Check made: a search of the packaged KJV for “morrow after the sabbath” and “morrow after the seventh sabbath” finds only Leviticus 23:11, 23:15 and 23:16; this is a word search, not a reading of every passage about the feast. These checked passages do not explicitly settle which sabbath is meant. The Hebrew quoted is the Westminster Leningrad Codex digital text. title: Seven sevens make forty-nine years; the jubile is the fiftieth. Where does the fiftieth year stand in the count?
summary: Every seventh year the land is not sown. Seven such sevens are forty-nine years, and then the fiftieth year is hallowed and not sown either. The chapter does not say whether the fiftieth year stands outside the sevens, making two unsown years in a row, or is counted as the first year of the next seven.
text: KJV Leviticus 25:4: “But in the seventh year shall be a sabbath of rest unto the land, a sabbath for the Lord: thou shalt neither sow thy field, nor prune thy vineyard.” KJV 25:8: “And thou shalt number seven sabbaths of years unto thee, seven times seven years; and the space of the seven sabbaths of years shall be unto thee forty and nine years.” KJV 25:10: “And ye shall hallow the fiftieth year, and proclaim liberty throughout all the land unto all the inhabitants thereof: it shall be a jubile unto you” KJV 25:11: “A jubile shall that fiftieth year be unto you: ye shall not sow, neither reap that which groweth of itself in it, nor gather the grapes in it of thy vine undressed.” KJV 25:20: “And if ye shall say, What shall we eat the seventh year? behold, we shall not sow, nor gather in our increase:” KJV 25:21: “Then I will command my blessing upon you in the sixth year, and it shall bring forth fruit for three years.” KJV 25:22: “And ye shall sow the eighth year, and eat yet of old fruit until the ninth year; until her fruits come in ye shall eat of the old store.” Hebrew (WLC) 25:8: תֵּ֥שַׁע וְאַרְבָּעִ֖ים שָׁנָֽה [forty-nine years]. 25:10: וְקִדַּשְׁתֶּ֗ם אֵ֣ת שְׁנַ֤ת הַחֲמִשִּׁים֙ שָׁנָ֔ה [and you shall hallow the year of the fiftieth year]. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) 25:8: ἐννέα καὶ τεσσαράκοντα ἔτη [forty-nine years]. 25:10: Καὶ ἁγιάσετε τὸ ἔτος τὸν πεντηκοστὸν ἐνιαυτὸν [and you shall hallow the year, the fiftieth year]. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/3/25/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/LEV25.htm.
reasoning: The forty-ninth year is a seventh year, so it is not sown. The fiftieth is the jubile and is not sown. If the fiftieth is a separate year after the forty-ninth, two years pass without sowing, and the next seven must start either at year fifty or at year fifty-one; the chapter says neither. The promise in 25:20–22 is given for “the seventh year”: the sixth year yields “for three years”, sowing resumes in “the eighth year”, and old store lasts “until the ninth”. No like provision is stated for a fiftieth year that follows an unsown forty-ninth. The length of the cycle, forty-nine years or fifty, depends on the answer, and land prices and the release of servants in the same chapter are reckoned by years to the jubile.
scope: Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. Readings, none of which the chapter states: the jubile is a fiftieth year standing outside the sevens, so that the cycle is fifty years and two fallow years fall together; the jubile is the fiftieth year and is also year one of the next seven, so that the cycle is forty-nine years; or “fiftieth” counts both ends, so that the jubile is the forty-ninth year itself. Check made: a search of the packaged KJV for “jubile” finds twenty verses, all in Leviticus 25 and 27 and Numbers 36:4, and a search for “fiftieth year” finds only Leviticus 25:10 and 25:11 besides two regnal dates in 2 Kings 15. Those verses were looked at; they speak of reckoning to the jubile and do not say how the count goes on after it. This is a word search, not a reading of every passage on the seventh year.
